acts.title: Six people, six right answers
text: Every one of the six speakers believes their own number of children is the ___ one.
The first has one, and rejects the idea that an only child is lonely and ___ .
The second has four, and says the physical strain is enormous and the joy ___ .
She also points out that an even number means nobody ever feels ___ .
The one with three says the real argument is relationships: three children means three ___ relationships.
Almost all of them use the same phrase — in ___ — which is worth noticing.

items.q: One of the top regrets is being mean to a ___ as a child.
Sometimes children have several ___.
I regret not ___ up to bullies at work.
Who in your family do you look ___ to?
I think I take ___ my father.
Who in your family tells you ___ the most?
One of my children may be able to ___ for me in my old age.
She is totally ___ to her children.

tts: Speaker one: Many parents have a second child for the sake of their first — to stop them being lonely and spoilt. But that is a stereotype, and I believe one child is ideal. Having one child has enabled me to devote plenty of time, money and energy to her. I also know that if I had had more children, I would have been less happy, as I would have had to give up too much.

Speaker two: I have four. I did not plan four, but in retrospect I now believe it is the perfect number. The physical strain of bringing up four is enormous, but the joy each one brings is immeasurable. Having an even number means each child has an automatic playmate; if two are playing together, the other ones have each other and do not feel left out.

Speaker three: I believe we have a responsibility to be mindful of the world’s growing population. I feel no couple should have more than two children — one to replace each parent. I read the other day that if every couple in a rich country had one fewer child, they would save nine thousand four hundred tonnes of carbon dioxide over their lifetime.

items.q: What are the speakers discussing?
o: How many children they think is the right number

items.q: Why does the first speaker believe one is ideal?
o: She can give her child more time, money and energy

items.q: What is the third speaker’s argument?
o: Each child puts extra pressure on the world’s resources

tts: Speaker four: I would like to make the case for not having children. Society puts a lot of pressure on us to have them, but it is not right for everyone. If I had had children, I would not have so much time now to devote to my husband and my career. I would have very little privacy, and my travels would be limited to school holidays.

Speaker five: I am in favour of having as many as you can manage. When you raise a large family — in my case seven — you create a little community that supports itself through the ups and downs of life. Friends often quote school fees as a reason not to. But if you are lucky enough to live in a country with great state schools, that is not an issue.

Speaker six: I did not mean to have three. The second of my pregnancies produced twins, and I ended up with what I believe is the ideal number. Three children means three sibling relationships, so if two of them fall out, at least they have another sibling to turn to.

items.s: Speaker four says society pressures people to have children.
She says her travel would be unaffected by having children.
Speaker five thinks a large family supports itself.
Speaker five says school fees are always a problem.
Speaker six planned to have three children.
Speaker six values the number of sibling relationships.

tts: If I had had more children, I would have been less happy.
If every couple had one fewer child, they would save nine thousand tonnes of carbon dioxide.

If two of them fall out, they have another sibling to turn to.

items.q: “If I had had more children, I would have been less happy.” When is this?
o: Entirely in the past — it did not happen

items.q: “If every couple had one fewer child, they would save…” When is this?
o: In the present or future, and it is not real

items.q: “If I had had children, I would not have so much time now.” What is unusual?
o: The condition is past and the result is present

items.q: “If two of them fall out, they have another sibling.” Why the present tense?
o: It is a real, general situation, not an unreal one

acts.title: Three unreal shapes, and the mixed one
rule: An unreal conditional imagines something that is not the case. English marks the unreality by stepping the tense back one further than the time you mean — a past form for the present, a past perfect for the past. Once you see that, the mixed conditional stops being a fourth rule and becomes an obvious combination of two.
points: if + past simple, would + infinitive. About now or the future, and not real. If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
if + past perfect, would have + past participle. About the past, and it did not happen.
if + past perfect, would + infinitive. If I had had children, I wouldn’t have so much time now.
if + past simple, would have + past participle. If I were more organized, I would have finished it.
If I were you is the standard form in writing, for every person.
could and might replace would when you want to be less certain: I might have gone.
eg: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
Second: unreal present.
If I were you, I would take the job.
Second, with were.
If I had had more children, I would have been less happy.
Third: unreal past.
If she had listened, none of this would have happened.
Third.
If I had had children, I wouldn’t have so much time now.
Mixed: past condition, present result.
If I were more organized, I would have finished it last week.
Mixed: present condition, past result.
I could have gone, but I didn’t.
could have, for possibility.
I might have said yes if she had asked earlier.
might have, less certain.
Had I known, I would have called.
Formal: if dropped, had moved to the front.
If two of them fall out, they have somebody to turn to.
Not unreal at all — a real general truth.
acts.careful: “If I would have known” is the commonest single error in this area. The if clause never takes would: it is “If I had known”.

Two facts. Now find the times.

4 · That is the mixed conditional. It is two rules, not a third one.

steps.cue: Rewrite it as a SECOND conditional

steps.cue: Now move it entirely into the past, as a THIRD conditional

items.from: She did not listen. All of this happened.

steps.cue: Rewrite it as a THIRD conditional

alt: If she had listened, none of this would have happened

steps.a: Had she listened none of this would have happened

items.from: Two of them fall out from time to time. There is always a third to turn to.

steps.cue: Write it as a REAL conditional, in the present
steps.a: If two of them fall out they have a third to turn to
alt: If two of them fall out, they have a third to turn to
steps.why: Not everything with if is unreal. A general truth stays in the present.

write.q: Write about 180 words on a decision in your family — yours or an older relative’s — and what would be different if it had gone the other way. Use the second conditional at least twice, the third at least twice, and one mixed conditional where a past decision explains a present situation.
plan: the decision, and who made it
what would be different now if it had gone otherwise
what you would do in their position
write.model:
In retrospect, the decision that shaped most of my family was my grandmother’s, and she never described it as a decision at all.

In 1974 she was offered a place at an institute in Novosibirsk and did not take it, because her mother was ill. If she had gone, none of us would be here — my parents met in a corridor of the factory where she worked instead.

If I had had that choice, I am fairly sure I would have gone, and I am not proud of being sure. She had four people depending on her; I have had a job I could leave.

What is strange is how present the decision still is. If she had taken the place, my father would not have grown up in that town, and I would not be writing this in Kazakh and Russian and English.

If I were her, at twenty-two, with that mother and that year, I do not know what I would do. That is the honest answer, and it took me until about thirty to reach it.
